terms.meaning: A named setting passed to the program from outside, such as a password or a switch.
A written description of what a valid set of settings looks like, used to check them.
A switch that turns a feature on or off without changing the code.

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: File setup
sections.what: Describes the file and brings in the schema library.
sections.why: The header says code should use the checked settings reader instead of reading raw values.
sections.watch_out: Code that reads raw environment values directly skips these checks.

sections.name: flag, optionalText
sections.title: Switch and optional text helpers
sections.what: Provides a helper that reads on and off style values with a default, and a helper that turns blank text into nothing.
sections.why: Likely reason: many settings are optional or on-off, so one shared helper keeps them consistent.
sections.watch_out: A value that is not one of the accepted on or off forms is rejected rather than guessed.

sections.name: baseSchema
sections.title: Settings schema
sections.what: Lists every setting, its default and its format. These include the database link, auth secret and URLs, admin emails, seeding and feature switches, prototype data, and outside service keys and models.
sections.why: The comments explain the empty auth URL handling and the reason for the design gallery setting, though the gallery comment conflicts with its default.
sections.watch_out: The design gallery comment says it is always on outside production, but the setting defaults to off, so this needs checking against the code that reads it.

sections.name: productionIssues, Env
sections.title: Production-only rules and the settings type
sections.what: Adds the production rules: the auth secret must be at least 32 characters, and seeding must be off. It also defines the final settings type, which adds the language model enabled flag.
sections.why: The comments give the reason for the secret rule and say seeding is destructive.
sections.watch_out: These rules are checked on raw values, so they still apply when another setting is invalid.

sections.name: parseEnv
sections.title: Full parse and prototype default
sections.what: Parses the raw settings with the schema and production rules, and throws one error listing every problem. It also turns prototype data off in production unless it is set explicitly, and turns the language model on only when a Gemini key is present.
sections.why: The comment says the prototype rule is in the architecture document, so it is intentional.
sections.watch_out: The language model flag depends only on the key, so a key with missing model names will still show as enabled here.

sections.name: env
sections.title: Cached settings access
sections.what: Parses the settings once and reuses the result. It also removes an empty auth URL from the process before the auth library reads it.
sections.why: The comment says this stops the auth library from failing on an empty URL.
sections.watch_out: Because the result is cached for the life of the process, changing the environment at runtime has no effect until restart.

summary: Reads and checks the app's environment settings once at startup, refusing to run if a required value is missing or invalid, and applying extra checks for production.
purpose: Makes the app fail early with a clear list of problems rather than failing later in an unclear way.
why: The header says the environment is checked at startup and code should use this instead of reading raw settings. The reason is stated in the code: a single validated source.
how: 1) Defines the expected settings, their defaults and their formats, such as a database link that must be a Postgres address. 2) Adds production-only rules, such as a minimum length for the auth secret and seeding forbidden. 3) Parses the raw settings and reports every problem together. 4) Turns prototype data off in production unless it is set on purpose. 5) Caches the result and removes an empty auth URL so the auth library does not fail.
inputs: The process environment values: database link, auth secret and URLs, admin emails, feature switches, and outside service keys and models.
outputs: A checked settings object, with a derived flag that says whether the language model is enabled. It throws one error listing every problem.
risks: Production refuses to start if the auth secret is too short or seeding is on. Feature switches default on for prototype data outside production. The settings are read once, so changes at runtime have no effect until restart.
debug: If the app will not start, read the error text: it lists each setting and what is wrong. If an admin or feature is not working, check the matching setting. If a value seems ignored, remember the settings are cached after the first read.
